evidence.correctness: Recomputed against sources the author did not write. (1) Kirsch polar stresses written out from Timoshenko & Goodier, Theory of Elasticity 3rd ed., sec. 35 (srr, stt, srt), rotated to Cartesian, compared with kirsch_stress at 50 random points: max abs diff 1.1e-15. (2) Hoop stress on the hole edge sigma(1-2cos2theta): von Mises 3.0 at 90 deg (Kt = 3), 1.0 at 0 and 45 deg, as expected. (3) Equilibrium by central differences at (1.7, 0.9): div sigma = -4e-11, 0. (4) Radial slope of the hoop stress at the top of the hole: by hand d/dr[sigma/2(2+a^2/r^2+3a^4/r^4)] at r=a = -7 sigma/a; code prints -7.000. (5) Rerun of experiments/run.py on a scratch copy (scikit-fem 12.0.2, 17.6 s): results.txt byte-identical to the committed file (diff empty), so every README table number reproduces. (6) Moving the outer boundary from R=10a to 20a at n_theta=32 changes the vertex peak 3.00131 -> 3.00134, confirming the exact-traction BC removes the finite-domain effect. The FE numbers are right. Two derived statements are not: the README says FE equals exact at the peak centroid 'to 0.03% or better at n_theta >= 16' but at 16 it is 0.129% (2.7495 vs 2.7530; 0.032% first at 32); and the 'bias/(slope*h)' column divides by the hoop slope 7 while the quantity sampled is von Mises, whose slope there is 8.5 (hoop 7 plus half the radial stress gradient 3, computed numerically -8.49998). With 8.5 the ratio is 0.296, 0.310, 0.329 at n=16, 32, 128 and the peak centroid's geometric offset is 0.317, 0.321, 0.332 h, i.e. it tends to the triangle-centroid value h/3, not the README's drifting '0.3-0.4 h'.

evidence.verification: Ran `python -m pytest -q tests`: 6 passed. Seeded 7 mutants in model.py with quality_mutate.py; all 7 caught: plane-stress lambda conversion removed, shear stress factor (1-nu)/2 -> (1-nu), outer normal ny zeroed, srt scaled 0.98, stress modulus scaled 1.004, centroid sample point 1/3 -> 0.30, x-traction scaled 1.01. The tests pin the exact solution (peak, traction-free edge, far field) and the FE behaviour (vertex within 1%, centroid below, rate, FE vs exact at centroid), which is strong for its size. Held at 3: the analysis in experiments/run.py (observed orders, bias/(slope*h), knock-down factors) has no test, and the slope-7 error lives there.
evidence.craft: Read src/simdesign_kirsch/model.py, __init__.py, tests/test_kirsch.py, experiments/run.py, figure.py. Compact and readable; DOF handling for P2 symmetry includes facet DOFs correctly. Minor: outer traction uses nx, ny = x/R, y/R evaluated on straight chords instead of the facet normal w.n (O(h^2), harmless here); writing v.value triggers 96 scikit-fem DeprecationWarnings (model.py:66); h_hole is the arc length, not the cell's radial size; dependencies unpinned in pyproject.toml, so 'reproduces exactly' depends on the scikit-fem version (12.0.2 reproduced). The hard-coded 7 in run.py:21 is the one substantive defect.
evidence.claims: Backed: table values (results.txt), field order 1.96-2.00, centroid order 0.81-0.98, vertex under 1% and order 1.6-2.0 for n>=8, knock-down factors 1.374...1.012, 'stresses do not depend on E', limitations section (one geometry, structured mesh with peak on a mesh line, polygonal hole), AI-assistance and simulation-only disclosures, Kirsch citation with an honest page-number caveat. Not backed: (a) README:35 '0.03% or better at n_theta >= 16' (0.13% at 16); (b) README:36 'the centroid effectively samples the stress about 0.3-0.4 h inside the edge ... drifts upward ... rough guide only' (an artefact of using the hoop slope 7 for a von Mises bias; the true offset is the fixed h/3); (c) README:38 'This explains the rising peak in the earlier L-bracket projects', contradicted by research/simdesign-meshmargin/README.md:44, which attributes that rise to sharp-corner singularities and a polygonal fillet, a divergent mechanism that centroid sampling bias at a smooth notch cannot explain.
evidence.fitness: Nearest prior work: the plate-with-a-hole is a standard FE verification benchmark (textbook exercises in Cook et al., Concepts and Applications of FEA; NAFEMS-style benchmarks), and the location of accurate stress sampling points and the low bias of centroid/Gauss-point peak readings are classical (Barlow 1976, 'Optimal stress locations in finite element models', IJNME 10:243; Zienkiewicz & Zhu 1992 superconvergent patch recovery, IJNME 33:1331). None is cited. The result (centroid reading first-order and low by about slope*h/3; boundary reading second-order) is what that literature predicts, so nothing here is new. A researcher can reuse the clean scripts as a verification harness, but against research/CLAUDE.md's bar (a programme aimed at a named venue) this is a sound homework-grade verification exercise. No baseline against the recovery methods practitioners actually use (nodal averaging, SPR), no unstructured mesh, no finite-width plate.
evidence.domain: Method follows verification practice: exact-solution boundary data, refinement sequence, observed order of accuracy (Roache / ASME V&V 20 style), with the limits stated. A senior FE analyst would sign off on the solver check but would object that (i) 'peak' in commercial practice is nodal-averaged or SPR-recovered stress, which is the comparison that would matter and is absent; (ii) the margin discussion ignores finite-width Kt (Howland 1930; Peterson's Stress Concentration Factors, where gross- and net-section Kt differ from 3 at practical d/W), which the README defers; (iii) the mechanism number (0.3-0.4 h) is misderived; (iv) the link to the L-bracket ignores the singular corners that dominate there.

verdict: The solver and the exact solution are right: the Kirsch formulas match Timoshenko & Goodier to 1e-15, the peak is exactly 3 sigma, the field is in equilibrium, and a rerun reproduces results.txt byte for byte; 7 of 7 seeded mutants in model.py are caught. It misses the bar on claims: the 'samples 0.3-0.4 h inside the edge' mechanism comes from dividing a von Mises bias by the hoop slope 7 instead of 8.5 (run.py:21; corrected, the offset is the fixed h/3), the 0.03%-at-n=16 statement is 0.13%, and the claim that this explains the L-bracket's rising peak contradicts meshmargin's own singularity diagnosis. As research it is a clean verification exercise whose result is the textbook expectation (Barlow 1976; Zienkiewicz-Zhu 1992, uncited) with no baseline against nodal averaging or SPR, far below the venue bar research/CLAUDE.md sets.
